segments.text: Okay, let's start the Q3 budget planning. Three things today: infrastructure costs, the GPU server purchase, and the second-half hiring budget.
In Q2 our AWS bill averaged $42K a month. That's 15% over budget, mostly EKS nodes and S3 egress.
For EKS, we could cut quite a bit by shutting down the dev cluster at night. A script that scales the node group down to zero overnight would save about $6K a month.
Nice. Ryan, could you roll that out by the end of July?
Sure, I'll have the nightly scale-down on the dev cluster by July 31.
Next, the GPU server. There's a request to buy a server with two H100s for internal LLM experiments. The quote is $98K per server.
Renting cloud GPUs costs more per hour, but we don't run experiments every day, so buying feels early. Let's use the cloud in Q3, watch the usage, and decide again in Q4.
Agreed. So we'll hold off on the GPU server purchase in Q3 and set aside $8K a month for cloud GPUs.
Last, the hiring budget. We want two backend developers and one ML engineer in the second half. Including job platform fees, that's about $120K for Q3.
The ML engineer is tied to the GPU decision, so let's start with just the two backend hires in Q3.
Okay, then Hannah from HR will post the job openings by this Friday.
To wrap up: the Q3 total is $510K for infrastructure and $120K for hiring. I'll send the budget to finance by next Tuesday. Thanks, everyone.

The H100 GPU server purchase is on hold; in Q3 we'll use cloud GPUs capped at $8K a month. Only the two backend developer hires go ahead. The Q3 total is $510K for infrastructure and $120K for hiring.

segments.text: Let's start the search API performance meeting. Search latency has been spiking since last week's deploy, so I want to pin down the cause and what we do about it.
On Grafana, p95 latency is usually 280 milliseconds, and now it's up to 1.2 seconds. It's worst during the traffic peak between 9 and 10 a.m.
Profiling shows that requests with wildcard queries in Elasticsearch eat 70% of the total time. Those queries came in with the autocomplete feature last week.
The standard fix for autocomplete is an edge n-gram analyzer instead of wildcards. It needs a reindex, but the index isn't big, so an hour or two should do it.
And I'd cache results for popular queries in Redis, with a TTL of about five minutes. Even a 60% hit rate would cut the peak load a lot.
Good. Then we'll switch autocomplete to edge n-grams and add a Redis cache for popular queries. The goal is to get p95 back under 300 milliseconds.
Jamie, please take the reindex and the analyzer change, and Tyler, the Redis cache. Both by next Wednesday, August 26.
Got it. But the real problem is that we only notice slowdowns like this after a deploy. Nothing catches them beforehand.
Right. Let's add a search regression test to CI, one that checks result correctness and latency for 200 representative queries. Ethan, could you own that?
Sure, I'll build the regression test suite and have it in CI by the first week of September.
Should we add a gate that blocks the deploy when latency goes over the threshold? Or just warn?
Warnings only for the first month, and if false alarms stay low, we switch to blocking deploys after that.
Sounds good. That's it for today.

summary.title: Search API latency fix
summary.summary: We covered the search API's p95 latency rising from 280 milliseconds to 1.2 seconds after last week's deploy. The cause was the Elasticsearch wildcard queries behind autocomplete. Autocomplete moves to an edge n-gram analyzer and popular queries get a Redis cache, to bring p95 back under 300 milliseconds. To prevent a repeat, a search regression test goes into CI; it only warns for the first month, then blocks deploys.

When latency exceeds the threshold, warn only for the first month, then block deploys

segments.text: Let's start the mobile app v2.4 release meeting. The big items this release are dark mode and the redesigned checkout screen. Today we need to lock the schedule and the QA scope.
Dark mode is about 90% done. Design sent changes for the checkout screen, so that needs about two more days.
The original release date was September 10, but because of the checkout screen, moving to September 17 seems safer. App Store review usually takes two to three days, too.
The holiday break starts September 24, so the 17th should be fine. It leaves time for hotfixes before the break.
Okay. Then the v2.4 release date is September 17.
The checkout changes are big, so we should widen the regression test scope. We especially need to check payment failures on older devices running iOS 16 or earlier.
Grace, please take the mobile regression tests. It'd be great to have the test case list by Tuesday, September 8.
Sure, I'll put together the regression test cases and share them by September 8. I'll run the checkout scenarios that aren't automated by hand.
We also need to look at accessibility for dark mode. A few screens had text contrast below the WCAG standard.
Sarah from the design team will send updated color tokens that meet the contrast standard by this Friday.
Last, crash reports. In Firebase Crashlytics the last version had a 99.2% crash-free rate. Let's aim for 99.5% or higher this time.
Okay, we'll add crash-free 99.5% or higher to the release criteria. Thanks, everyone.

Dark mode text contrast falls short of WCAG, so new color tokens are coming. Crash-free 99.5% or higher is now a release criterion.

segments.text: Let's start the Q4 budget and OKR meeting. We'll review Q3 spending first, then adjust the Q4 budget.
We budgeted $510K for Q3 infrastructure and actually spent $460K. The nightly scale-down made a big difference, and we used fewer cloud GPUs than expected.
On the other hand, LLM API costs are new. The customer support summary feature cost $15K in September alone, and it could reach $25K a month in Q4.
At that level we should switch to a smaller model or add caching. I hear prompt caching can cut it by 30 to 40%.
Okay, then let's cap the Q4 LLM API budget at $20K a month and automatically switch to a smaller model above that.
Leadership agreed to cut the marketing budget by 20% in Q4. That means canceling one in-person event.
Too bad, but I agree. We'll cancel the booth at the November developer conference and run an online webinar instead.
We should also revisit the GPU server purchase. Q3 cloud GPU usage averaged about $3K a month, so the case for buying is weaker now.
Then no GPU server purchase this year. We'll look at it again in Q1 next year.
I've narrowed the OKRs to three: keep search p95 latency at 300 milliseconds, mobile crash-free at 99.5%, and onboard three new customers.
Great. Mark from finance will finalize the Q4 budget by September 30.
The ML engineer hire stays on hold in Q4, and one of the two backend hires has already joined, so we'll only fill the remaining one.
I'll post the OKR doc to Confluence by tomorrow. Thanks, everyone.

With marketing cut by 20%, the November developer conference booth is canceled in favor of a webinar. There is no GPU server purchase this year, and the OKRs are search p95 latency at 300 milliseconds, crash-free 99.5%, and three new customers onboarded.

segments.text: Let's start the Bluepeak Logistics onboarding meeting. Today we want to agree on three things: SLA terms, how data gets integrated, and the onboarding schedule.
The customer wants 99.9% availability and a guaranteed response time under 500 milliseconds for the shipment tracking API, even at peak hours.
99.9% is fine with our current infrastructure, but 500 milliseconds is tight if it's p99. Contracting on p95 is more realistic.
Then we'll propose a p95 500 millisecond response-time SLA, with a 10% credit on the monthly fee if we miss it.
For integration, the customer wants to upload CSVs over SFTP every day, but we'd rather recommend the REST API and webhooks.
We agreed on a phased approach: daily SFTP CSV batches for the first three months, then webhooks once things are stable.
For onboarding, kickoff is October 13 and go-live is the first week of November. The customer will send test data by October 10.
We also need an incident contact plan. The customer wants a 24-hour hotline, but outside weekday business hours we have a single on-call engineer.
Then only Sev1 incidents get a 24-hour response, and everything else is handled the next business day. Let's put that in the contract.
Chloe from business development, please draft the contract and send it to the customer by October 7.
Sure, I'll include the SLA terms and the incident scope and send it by October 7.
Justin from technical support will have the integration API docs and a sandbox account ready before kickoff. That's it for today.

Integration starts with daily SFTP CSV batches for three months, then moves to webhooks. Only Sev1 incidents get a 24-hour response. Kickoff is October 13, with go-live in the first week of November.
